goal_text: Write a PRD for my side project

nodes.title: Nail the problem you're solving
nodes.one_liner: What pain exists, for whom, and why it matters

nodes.title: Who is this actually for?
nodes.one_liner: Defining your target user and their context

nodes.title: What does success look like?
nodes.one_liner: Goals and signals that tell you it worked

nodes.title: Draw the scope boundary
nodes.one_liner: The core thing you're committing to build

nodes.title: Write the 'Out of Scope' list
nodes.one_liner: What you're deliberately NOT building, and why

nodes.title: Spell out the core user flow
nodes.one_liner: Key actions a user takes, start to finish

nodes.title: Surface your assumptions and open questions
nodes.one_liner: Unknowns and bets baked into your thinking

outline.rationale: The user wants to learn PRD-writing as a thinking tool to force scope clarity on a solo side project. I front-load the "thinking" sections that drive scope clarity (problem, user, success) and make scope itself a two-node treatment: an explicit in-scope core and a dedicated out-of-scope node, since the user named scope clarity as the real payoff and "what's explicitly out" is where most scope creep gets killed. The user flow node grounds the abstract scope in concrete behavior. Assumptions/open-questions and rough priorities round out the genuine PRD thinking work without drifting into process formalities. I deliberately omitted stakeholder sign-off, release/launch logistics, metrics dashboards, team-communication framing, and any 'what is a PRD' basics — all deprioritized per the confirmed understanding (solo, thinking-tool, already knows the project). Structure stays domain-general since the project specifics weren't given. Nodes are MECE: problem vs. user vs. success vs. in-scope vs. out-of-scope vs. flow vs. assumptions vs. priorities have low content overlap.
